newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik govt forces renew attack on rebel colonel.
newsitem.headline: Tajik govt forces renew attack on rebel colonel.

text.p: Tajik government forces shelled positions held by rebel Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev south of the capital Dushanbe on Tuesday, shortly after the mutinous colonel accused them of scuttling peace talks with an air raid.

In the village of Kirov, about 18 km (12 miles) south of Dushanbe, the presidential guard unleashed clutches of Grad rockets every few minutes on the fourth day of fighting in the volatile former Soviet republic.

The troops said Khudoyberdyev's men were returning fire with mortars. "We exchanged some fire earlier today but we began rocketing their positions at about 3.30 p.m. (1030 GMT)," said a government commander about 14 km (nine miles) south of Dushanbe.

The commander of an elite government armoured brigade who has mutinied on two previous occasions, Khudoyberdyev moved his armour towards Dushanbe at the weekend in the wake of heavy fighting between two rival warlords in the Tajik capital.
Earlier on Tuesday, Khudoyberdyev told Reuters by telephone that government aircraft had bombed the town of Kalininabad, near his headquarters about 120 km (80 miles) south of Dushanbe.

"Today, at 10 a.m. (0500 GMT), I was supposed to negotiate with the head of the CIS (Commonwealth of Independent States) peacekeeping force but government aircraft bombed Kalininabad this morning," said Khudoyberdyev.
"I don't think the negotiations will take place," the 34-year-old rebel colonel told Reuters by telephone from his base near the southern town of Kurgan Tyube.
But a spokesman in Dushanbe for the predominantly Russian peacekeeping force in the central Asian republic told Reuters that no talks had been scheduled.

Russia has 20,000 troops in Tajikistan, which form the bulk of the Commonwealth of Independent States' peacekeeping force. It has ruled out any hasty involvement in violence which flared just weeks after a four-year civil war formally ended.

"The collective peacekeeping force strictly observes a position of neutrality and non-interference in the internal affairs of sovereign Tajikistan," said a statement from the commander of the CIS troops which was handed to reporters.
"Its units are at their permanent bases and take no part in the armed conflict and its liquidation."
Western observers see the Russian troops, which also guard the frontier with war-torn Afghanistan, as the main guarantee of the embattled President Imomali Rakhmonov's survival.
On Sunday, Rakhmonov issued a three-day ultimatum to the rebel colonel to lay down his arms or face "destruction".
Kalininabad, some 120 km (80 miles) south of the capital Dushanbe, is close to Khudoyberdyev's headquarters. He did not say whether there had been any casualties in the air raid.
Khudoyberdyev lost a strategically important aluminium smelter west of Dushanbe to Rakhmonov's guard on Monday. An armed stand-off ensued and continued on Tuesday.

The rebel commander said he was ready to return to barracks if the presidential guard did likewise. "I agree to peace talks and I want peace in Tajikistan...If the presidential guard go back to barracks, my forces will return to Kurgan Tyube".

Khudoyberdyev, regarded by Western diplomats as politically ambitious, has not revealed his goals. "I'm not trying to move on Dushanbe," Khudoyberdyev said. "Government forces provoked us by moving toward Kurgan Tyube -- we had to defend ourselves".
The outbreak of fighting has no connection with Tajikistan's armed Islamic opposition, with whom the government signed a peace accord in June aimed at ending four years of civil war.
War and instability in Tajikistan, a mountainous country of 5.7 million people, have carved the republic into fiefdoms under the control of maverick armed groups much like in Afghanistan.
